strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between visual input and internal parametric knowledge, extending mechanistic interpretability work from language models to the multimodal setting.

It introduces WHOOPs-AHA!, a controlled dataset built from WHOOPs! with GPT-4o-generated factual/counterfactual continuations and manual verification, specifically designed to induce and analyze cross-modal knowledge conflicts.

The methodology is multi-pronged and generally rigorous: logit lens for component-level localization, head-level analysis, targeted causal interventions on attention heads, random-head and random-patch controls, and comparison of attention-based vs gradient-based visual attribution.

The main findings are consistent across two models (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b): attention blocks and a small subset of late-layer attention heads favor counterfactual visual context, while MLP blocks favor factual knowledge; targeted interventions causally shift predictions, and attention attribution identifies counterfactual-driving image regions more sharply than gradients.
The paper is clear and well-structured, with informative figures, qualitative examples, and a useful discussion of limitations and ethical considerations.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: the dataset and code are released, prompts are provided, model versions and hardware/compute details are reported, and control experiments strengthen confidence in the central causal claims.
weaknesses: The dataset is small and simplified: only 436 examples for LLaVA-NeXT and 432 for Gemma3, with one factual and one counterfactual token per instance. This limits statistical reliability and generality, and many comparative claims lack significance tests.

The evaluation reduces knowledge conflict to next-token logit comparisons between a single factual and counterfactual token, rather than full generation or broader downstream behavior; this may not capture the full complexity of cross-modal conflict resolution.

The mechanistic analysis is localized to the final token position and attention/MLP blocks, leaving the visual encoder and broader circuit-level mechanisms largely unexplored, as the authors acknowledge.

The logit lens is an approximate diagnostic known to introduce distortions, yet it is central to the head-selection and component-localization analyses; conclusions should be interpreted with that caveat.

Attention-head selection is post hoc on the same dataset used for intervention. Random-head controls help, but the causal interpretation remains specific to the chosen intervention design and may not generalize to other conflict types or architectures.

The attribution comparison against gradient-based methods relies mainly on ablation curves and qualitative examples, without formal precision/recall metrics, human evaluation, or comparison to other attribution methods such as attention rollout or integrated gradients.

Novelty is partially constrained by concurrent work on visual counterfactuals and steering in VLMs; the paper differentiates itself but the conceptual advance is incremental relative to prior knowledge-conflict and interpretability work.

Dataset construction relies on GPT-4o generation and manual filtering, with no reported inter-annotator agreement or analysis of potential generation artifacts, which could affect the reliability of factual/counterfactual token labels.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between visual evidence and internal parametric knowledge. The framing around counterfactual image-text pairs is clear and well motivated.

The introduced WHOops-AHA! dataset is carefully constructed by pairing visually anomalous images with commonsense prompts and factual/counterfactual continuations, and it is released for research use. The dataset construction pipeline, including GPT-4o generation prompts and manual verification, is documented.

The methodology is multi-pronged and generally rigorous: logit lens analysis localizes the conflict, attention-head attribution identifies candidate components, targeted interventions establish causal influence, and ablation experiments test the functional importance of identified visual patches.

The finding of a functional separation between attention blocks (favoring counterfactual/visual context) and MLP blocks (favoring factual knowledge) is consistent across LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b, strengthening confidence in the result.

The causal intervention experiments are convincing: reweighting factual/counterfactual attention heads shifts model behavior in the expected directions, while random-head controls show no comparable effect. The paper also checks generation quality degradation and constrains intervention strength accordingly.

The attention-based attribution method is shown to identify causally important image regions more effectively than gradient-based attribution in the ablation experiments, and the qualitative examples help illustrate the localized nature of counterfactual visual signals.
The paper is clearly written, includes useful appendices, discusses limitations candidly, and provides sufficient reproducibility details (models, prompts, compute, released code/data).
weaknesses: The dataset is relatively small (hundreds of examples after filtering) and relies on GPT-4o generation plus manual verification. There is little detail on inter-annotator agreement, annotation guidelines, or how subjective the factual/counterfactual token choices are, which may limit reproducibility and generality.

The mechanistic analysis is confined to the final token position and uses logit lens projections from intermediate layers, which is an approximate diagnostic rather than a full causal tracing of information flow across layers and token positions. This limits the strength of claims about the precise mechanism.

Only two open-source VLM architectures are studied. While the consistency across them is a strength, the findings may not generalize to other model families, scales, or proprietary VLMs with different vision encoders and fusion mechanisms.

The claim that attention attribution outperforms gradient-based attribution in “precision” is not evaluated against ground-truth localized regions. The ablation metric measures causal importance for restoring factual accuracy, not localization precision or recall, so the wording overstates the evidence.

The intervention is a coarse multiplicative reweighting of attention over entire image/text token groups at the final token position. It does not isolate individual head-specific token interactions, and MLP components are not causally intervened upon despite being implicated in factual recall.

The work overlaps significantly with concurrent studies on knowledge conflicts and steering in VLMs. The novelty lies mainly in applying a known framework to multimodal conflict with a new dataset and a specific attribution comparison, which may be incremental relative to existing interpretability work.

There is no evaluation of whether the identified heads or visual regions generalize across tasks, datasets, or prompt formulations beyond WHOops-AHA!, nor are prompt sensitivity and stochasticity of the dataset generation process fully characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between internal factual knowledge and counterfactual visual input, which is directly connected to hallucination and interpretability research.
It introduces WHOops-AHA!, a controlled counterfactual dataset derived from WHOops! with factual and counterfactual continuations, and promises public code and data.
The analysis covers two VLMs (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b) and includes appendix results for the second model, which strengthens the empirical breadth relative to single-model studies.

The paper combines multiple mechanistic tools (Logit Lens, attention-head localization, targeted attention intervention, attention-based and gradient-based attribution, patch ablation) to triangulate the phenomenon.

It reports a clear functional separation: attention blocks tend to support the counterfactual visual context, whereas MLP blocks tend to support internal factual knowledge, with layer-wise trends that are broadly consistent with prior LLM interpretability work.
It identifies a small subset of attention heads whose attention patterns differ by modality and includes a random-head control experiment to support the specificity of the identified heads.
The qualitative examples in Figure 6 are intuitive and help illustrate that attention-based attribution can highlight semantically relevant image regions driving counterfactual predictions.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper includes some reproducibility details (hardware, libraries, compute time) and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: The central causal intervention is methodologically problematic as described. Equations (4) and (5) apply multiplicative factors (1+λ) and (1-λ) to post-softmax attention weights. For λ > 1 or λ < -1, one of these factors becomes negative, and no renormalization or clamping is described. Since the paper uses λ ∈ [-3, 3] and Figure 4 varies λ from -2 to 2, the described intervention would produce invalid attention distributions. This undermines reproducibility and the validity of the causal steering claim.

The sign/direction of the intervention is inconsistent across the paper. The equations, the text in Section 4.3, and the Figure 4 caption do not agree on whether λ > 0 boosts factual heads and weakens counterfactual heads or the opposite. As written, it is impossible to determine exactly what intervention was applied.

The dataset construction relies heavily on GPT-4o generation, and although the authors state that all content was manually verified, they provide no details on the number of annotators, verification criteria, inter-annotator agreement, or rejection rate. This limits confidence in dataset quality and reproducibility.

The evaluation is small (≈436 examples for LLaVA and ≈432 for Gemma3) and relies on a single factual and counterfactual token per example. It does not evaluate full generations systematically, so the claims about controlling model behavior are stronger than the evidence supports.

The attribution comparison is not rigorously quantified. The paper claims that attention-based attribution outperforms gradient-based attribution in precision, but there is no ground-truth localization metric (e.g., IoU with annotated anomaly regions), no statistical testing, and the supporting evidence is mainly ablation curves and qualitative examples.

The WHOops! images are synthetic/composited and visually implausible. This raises the concern that the observed 'visual override' may be driven by low-level image artifacts or unnatural composition rather than genuine semantic knowledge conflict, which weakens the interpretation of the mechanism.

Novelty is incremental: the work extends Ortu et al. (2024) from text-only LMs to VLMs and applies established Logit Lens and attention-head intervention techniques. The concurrent work by Golovanevsky et al. (2025a), acknowledged in the paper, already studies steering vectors for modality competition, reducing the distinctiveness of the contribution.

The selection of 20 heads and the threshold τ is not accompanied by a systematic sensitivity analysis or held-out validation. It is also unclear whether the factual and counterfactual head sets overlap, which would complicate the interpretation of the intervention.

There are reproducibility gaps: the code/dataset link is not visible in the manuscript text (only a GitHub icon), and the derived dataset is released under non-commercial terms, which may restrict reuse.

Some claims are overstated. The intervention degrades generation quality at higher |λ| (Table 1, KL divergence), so it is not a clean control mechanism; the paper itself acknowledges this only in the limitations. The phrase 'outperforming gradient-based attribution in precision' is not directly measured against ground-truth counterfactual regions.

There is an apparent inconsistency/ambiguity in reporting head preferences: the text states that counterfactual heads favor t_cofa '15% of the time', which does not clearly support the claimed strong alignment with their respective information sources.

strengths: Introduces WHOOPs-AHA!, a controlled multimodal counterfactual dataset for mechanistic analysis of knowledge conflicts, with dataset and code released for reproducibility.
Provides a clear functional separation between attention blocks (biased toward counterfactual visual context) and MLP blocks (biased toward factual parametric knowledge) in two open VLMs.

Identifies a small set of upper-layer attention heads that mediate the conflict and demonstrates causal control through targeted attention interventions, including random-head controls and bidirectional steering.
Shows conflict-specificity: suppressing the identified counterfactual heads' image attention does not degrade POPE accuracy, indicating these heads are not generic visual processors.
Demonstrates that attention-based attribution localizes counterfactual image regions more precisely than gradient and random baselines using SAM segmentation masks, with statistical support.
Generalizes the head identification and intervention results to an independently constructed visual counterfactual dataset, suggesting transferability across datasets.
The paper is generally clear, well-structured, and reproducible, with model choices, compute details, prompts, and validation procedures documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Dataset construction and quality control rely heavily on GPT-4o and LLM-as-a-judge; the small human validation (20 items) shows low exact agreement for knowledge/anomaly alignment (35% text-only, 65% image), raising concerns about dataset reliability.

The core mechanistic evaluation is limited to next-token factual-vs-counterfactual logits in two late-fusion VLMs; generalization to other architectures, free-form generation, and broader conflict types remains untested.

The visual attribution comparison uses only 20 images and one segmentation method; for LLaVA the advantage over gradient-based attribution is modest, so the claim of more precise attribution is narrower than stated.

The intervention modifies attention only at the final token position and does not establish that the identified heads are necessary or sufficient for conflict resolution in natural full-sequence generation.

Head selection and evaluation share the same Logit Lens probe, which may introduce selection bias; the choice of 20 heads appears somewhat tuned, and sensitivity to this hyperparameter is not fully explored.
The Logit Lens technique is known to introduce approximation errors, and although acknowledged, the main conclusions depend on this approximate diagnostic.

strengths: Introduces WHOOPS-AHA!, a controlled dataset for studying conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and contradictory visual evidence, with factual/counterfactual token annotations and a documented construction pipeline.

Applies Logit Lens and targeted attention-head interventions to two VLM architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B), identifying a small subset of upper-layer attention heads that mediate factual versus counterfactual predictions.

Provides causal evidence via bidirectional attention-head interventions: boosting factual heads shifts predictions toward parametric knowledge, suppressing counterfactual heads shifts toward visual evidence, and random-head controls show no comparable effect.
Reports a functional dissociation between attention and MLP blocks: attention blocks favor visual context while MLP blocks favor factual knowledge, with consistent patterns across both models.
Demonstrates generalization of identified heads to an independently constructed visual counterfactual dataset and shows overlap between the top heads, supporting mechanism transferability.

Proposes an attention-based visual attribution method using conflict-resolution heads and validates it with ablation and segmentation-based metrics, showing improved localization over random baselines and, especially for Gemma3, over gradient-based attribution.
Reproducibility is supported by released code and dataset, detailed prompts, compute requirements, and appendix experiments on model variants, POPE controls, and intervention parameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: The attention-head intervention modifies post-softmax attention weights without showing renormalization (Equations 1-2), so attention rows no longer sum to 1; this could distort model behavior and confound the causal interpretation unless the implementation renormalizes or the intervention is reframed as a controlled perturbation.

Head selection and main evaluation are performed on the same dataset, creating a risk of selection/evaluation circularity. The generalization experiment on Visual CounterFact helps, but a held-out split for head selection and evaluation would strengthen the main causal claims.

Human validation of dataset quality is limited to 20 items, and exact agreement between LLM judges and human raters is low (35-70%), although adjacent agreement is high. The factual/counterfactual token validity and overall dataset quality therefore rest substantially on LLM-as-a-judge judgments.

The attribution claim that attention from conflict-resolution heads is more accurate than gradient-based methods is only clearly supported for Gemma3. For LLaVA-NeXT the improvement is small (median 2.05 vs. 1.88) and based on only 20 images, so the abstract's unqualified claim overstates the evidence.

The MLP-versus-attention functional separation is primarily correlational; MLP interventions on the last three blocks produce only marginal changes, so the causal role of MLPs in conflict resolution is not fully established.

Factual and counterfactual token sets are generated by GPT-4o and may not always match the target model's internal parametric knowledge. Filtering and validation address this partly, but the construction could still introduce tokens that are not genuinely factual or counterfactual for LLaVA-NeXT/Gemma3.

The analysis is restricted to late-fusion LLaVA-style models, which limits the generality of conclusions about VLM conflict resolution. The authors acknowledge this, but broader claims about VLM mechanisms remain constrained.
The main intervention results (Figure 4) and ablation curves (Figure 5) lack error bars or statistical tests across seeds/samples, making it difficult to assess robustness beyond the reported trends.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and contradictory visual evidence, with a focus on mechanistic interpretability rather than only behavioral evaluation.
It introduces WHOOP AHA!, a controlled counterfactual dataset built from WHOOPs! with factual and counterfactual completions, and provides code/data release and a reproducibility statement.

The experimental pipeline is coherent: logit inspection identifies candidate factual and counterfactual attention heads, targeted interventions shift factual accuracy, and control experiments with random heads and MLP interventions help test specificity.

The finding that attention blocks tend to favor visual/counterfactual evidence while MLP blocks favor internal factual knowledge is consistent across LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3, and aligns with prior work on factual recall in MLPs.

The paper includes useful additional evidence: generalization to Visual CounterFact, a POPE control suggesting the identified counterfactual heads are not generic vision-processing heads, and quantitative attribution analysis against gradient and random baselines.
The writing is generally clear, with limitations and ethical considerations discussed, and the paper is relevant to ACL/CL audiences interested in multimodal interpretability and hallucination.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is largely token-level: factual accuracy is measured as whether the logit of a preselected factual token exceeds that of a preselected counterfactual token at the final position. This does not establish that the model's generated outputs are steered in open-ended generation, yet the abstract and conclusion claim to 'steer the model' and alter 'model outputs.'

The attention-head intervention modifies image and text attention weights multiplicatively without clearly renormalizing the attention distribution. This confounds relative modality weighting with overall attention magnitude, so the causal interpretation that the identified heads specifically mediate factual-vs-visual competition is not fully isolated.

Head identification and intervention are performed on the same dataset and examples, with no held-out validation of head selection. This risks overfitting/selection bias and makes the reported intervention gains harder to interpret as a stable mechanism.

The attribution comparison is based on only 20 images and may be partly circular: the heads are selected because they favor the counterfactual token, and then their attention is used to localize the counterfactual object. The gradient baseline is also not strongly tuned or defended, making the claim of 'more precise attribution' tentative.

Dataset quality control relies on LLM-as-a-judge with only 20 human-validated items; the reported exact agreement for text-only knowledge alignment is low (35%), which raises concerns about the reliability of the factual/counterfactual token labels.

The MLP intervention control is not comparable in specificity to the attention-head intervention (it modifies broad residual streams in the last three blocks), so the conclusion that conflicts are 'primarily mediated by attention mechanisms' rather than MLPs is not adequately supported.

The per-head logit-lens/direct-logit-attribution procedure is not described in sufficient technical detail, and its validity for individual attention heads in these architectures is not established, creating reproducibility concerns.

Main intervention results lack statistical tests or error bars, and the choice of the number of heads (20) and intervention strength λ is partly heuristic. This weakens confidence in the robustness of the reported effects.

The claim that the identified heads are conflict-specific rather than generic visual heads is tested mainly by suppressing counterfactual heads on POPE; factual heads are not similarly tested, leaving the specificity argument incomplete.

Several limitations are acknowledged in the appendix, but some of the paper's broader claims are not sufficiently tempered in the main text, giving the impression of stronger conclusions than the token-level evidence supports.
